I hear this all the time.

Video games need another market crash.

Video games are inevitably headed towards another market crash.

The low quality of triple AAA titles is the same as E.T, meaning we're going to have a dropoff of market interest, thus causing a crash.

What I would like to do is put a couple things in perspective regarding the great crash and the current market of games as it relates to that. I was inspired to do so from this article on linkedin's website. I suggest you go read it to get some perspective on the issue. I will point out a few things about this article that I find very disagreeable.

In the "Parallels Today" section, the author mentions the first point as being paralleled today with too many platforms rather than consoles. I think this is a huge difference, especially considering how he rightfully notes how computers picked up the difference after the 1983 (not 1985) market crash. The problem had much more to do with games companies trying to cover these wide range of systems, and most importantly, the fact that these systems internally were widely different. The three primary platforms of the day - the Colecovision, the Intellivision, and the Atari - all had wildly different ports of the same games. This required more programming manpower. Nowadays you can look up how to port one thing to another, accounting only for processing power in the end.

Next is the mention of high profile failures. We all know that AAA publishers are spending too much money to make games. That has been evident since the Playstation era. However, that doesn't mean that smash hits aren't making returns. He mentions Sim City, but that game still sold gangbusters. A sale is a sale, and though eroding customer trust is bad, you're not losing millions on licensing deals like the things that he's referring to. In fact, companies like EA make their meat through things like FIFA and Madden, despite making their hardcore communities ever the more angry with each installment.

One point that I'm going to try and get across very strongly in my video series is that "E.T" was not the "catalyst" for the video game crash. Not even close. It was a compounding money sink against bigger and bigger money sinks, thus leading to what happened when Jack Tramiel bought the company. People may have been disappointed with games, but to cause the mass customer exodus that happened needs to be caused more by disinterest than passion.

I certainly see signs of a decline in this console generation. Even judging by the time of the current generation (a word I don't like to use often), there are far less consoles in people's houses than the prior years. I don't think that by itself is a reason to call the crash imminent though. Not only are things in place to reel back from a market crash (which is not at all like the Crash of 1929 in most cases), but it won't be as effective with markets aimed towards more attentive consumers, since they're not going to just stop playing games. Games back in the day were a novelty, and when they couldn't advance and meet a price point, parents stopped buying them.

I don't think most of the claims vying for a market crash to come sometime soon are very valid. The only possible platform I could see it for is mobile devices, and that's not going to make handhelds or PC gaming dip. They are completely different markets with different priorities. Consoles were the only true game in town back in 1983, and PCs only barely managed to fill the gap in the four years until the NES made North American markets fully viable again. That is another issue not addressed here: International markets. The North American Video Game Crash of 1983 was just that. Japan and the equally important Europe did not see its affects, though Britain specifically suffered an unrelated dip in '84.

It's hard to surmise the state of the video game industry at any given point in history, thus remains one of my goals with my video series. If you have any opinions or perspective on the matter, feel free to post below. I shall leave with some discussion points.

When do you consider the 1983 Video Game Crash to have ended, and why?

What's your objective view of the state of the market? Is it truly as on edge as analysts and hardcore gamers claim?

Which platforms do you actively engage on? How many games do you have for each platform and how much money do you spend?

Oh FFS. Mercury switches are ridiculously common.. They were commonly used in old, mechanical thermostats, so there was a time where damn near every house in the US had them. Heat-only models had one mercury switch. Heat/cool models typically had two. Heat Pump models typically had at least three, if not more.

A mercury switch is a glass vial with two electrical contacts and a blob of mercury inside. That's it. Absurdly simple, ingenious design. Tilting the switch determines whether the mercury makes or breaks contact. In thermostats, the switch is attached to a bimetallic strip that flexes based on temperature. Mercury switches are the early, ultra-simplistic versions of the accelerometers we have in every phone, Wiimote, etc. There's nothing inherently dangerous about them. Possessing them is certainly not indicative of intent to build a bomb.
